source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
Forty megawatts at CyrusOne's Durham campus is 80 percent of all data center capacity North Carolina has disclosed, and 14 of the state's 19 mapped facilities disclose none at all.

The pattern is a disclosure gap rather than a capacity gap. Five North Carolina facilities publish megawatt figures, and those five are the only ones that can be counted. For AI, published IT capacity is one of the few public handles on where compute can physically sit, and in this state that handle covers a minority of the mapped sites. A single campus dominating the disclosed total says more about who publishes than about where the load actually is.

The 40 megawatts come from the operator's own specification page. That same page does not state the power infrastructure serving the site, the PUE, the grid operator for Durham, or any power purchase agreement. Without those, the figure describes what the building is provisioned for, not what it draws or what the local grid will permit it to draw. That gap between provisioned and permitted is where AI scaling actually gets decided.

What the data does not cover matters as much as what it does. There are no certifications, no breakdown by workload or tenant class, and no announced expansion, which the suitability score of 69 lists as its missing input. Any accelerator count derived from 40 megawatts depends on assumed rack density and assumed power per GPU, neither of which the operator publishes. The campus's relevance to AI training specifically is not established here, only its size relative to a mostly silent state.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
